questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -4 \\ -1 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -1)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-3.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -9 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-16) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -15) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )(\lambda +3)(\lambda -5) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Note that all $\lambda $'s are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial.

Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & a & -2 \\ -1 & b & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $(a+b)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 12 & -10 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st  and the $2$nd ones). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get  ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $(a+b)^{2}=(0+1)^{2}=1.$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -4 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a & 1 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $a-b.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-8,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -4 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=1-1=0.$
